title: Come apart and rest (Mark 6:30–44)
hookLine: come apart into a desert place, and rest a little, then the crowds, then the loaves

cards: Exams done. The shift over. The move finished, the guests gone.
Then comes that strange hour, buzzing and exhausted at once, a hundred stories and no energy to tell them. The twelve come back from their first mission like that.

They crowd around Jesus to report everything they did and taught. It's so busy, Mark says, with people coming and going, that they don't even have time to eat. And Jesus answers with an invitation, not a new assignment.

teach.b: First, the invitation. In the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat." Apart means away, by yourselves.
Jesus sees tired people and prescribes rest before anything else: an invitation from him, not a reward they've earned. Second, the crowd.
They take a boat to find a quiet place, but people see them go, run around the shore on foot, and get there first. The rest is interrupted.
And Jesus, seeing the crowd, has compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he teaches them. Third, the loaves.
It gets late. The disciples say, send them away to buy food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat.
They have five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass, takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to hand out.
Everyone eats and is filled, and they gather up twelve baskets of leftovers. Five thousand men were fed.
Fourth, those four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave.

teach.h: COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE, AND REST.
teach.b: Catholics hear them again at every Mass, in the words over the bread at the Last Supper, so this meal in the desert points forward to the Eucharist.
And notice where it started: the meal on the green grass grew out of a break that never quite happened.

how: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, and a retreat, days apart for prayer and rest, is sometimes framed with this passage as its invitation.

o: together, as one crowd, all at once

games.q: what's inside the reading — tap the pairs.

s: the twelve got a long, quiet rest
the crowds ran ahead and got there first. the rest was interrupted.
Jesus took, blessed, broke and gave the loaves
the same four actions Catholics hear at every Mass.
the disciples wanted to send the crowd away to buy food
Jesus answered: you give them something to eat.

games.q: your friends are back from a long mission, so busy they haven't eaten. what does Jesus say to them?
o: well done; now go out again.
come apart into a desert place, and rest a little.
tell the crowds everything you did.
games.why: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little." rest comes before anything else.

practice: This is your desert place: no one coming or going for two minutes. Let your eyes close or soften, and notice how tired you actually are, without judging it.
If you pray, hear the invitation as if it were spoken to you, come apart, and rest a little; if you don't, just rest a little, the way you'd tell a tired friend to.

wordCard.voice: Kat' idian. Greek for apart, privately, by yourselves, Jesus's invitation to his tired friends, before the crowds and before the loaves. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: apart, privately, by yourselves, in Jesus's invitation to rest.

carryVoice: Your line: rest a little. The invitation came before the bread. That's two hundred eight.
